lessons.explanation: The reviewer was told to make sure error handling is "robust", which leaves it to decide what matters, so it comments on logging, `catch` width and retries. Naming what to report (swallowed exceptions, failed charges recorded as successful) and what to skip gives it explicit criteria, so the comments that remain are ones developers act on.

a.reasoning: Explicit categories to report and to skip replace the vague word that caused the noise. The reviewer no longer has to guess which error-handling problems matter, so precision rises without losing the real defects.

b.reasoning: Explicit criteria are the right kind of fix, but this list names the very nitpicks developers are muting: logging, wide `catch` blocks and retry wrappers. Criteria that include them keep the noise and give it structure.
b.tempting: It is explicit and categorical, which is exactly what the guide recommends.

c.reasoning: A stronger model still has no definition of the team's standard, so it would still guess. Fixing the prompt comes before paying for a bigger model, and the switch adds cost while the ambiguity stays.
c.tempting: A smarter model should judge better what counts as robust error handling.

d.reasoning: A keyword filter hides the noise but also drops a genuine finding that happens to mention logging, such as a swallowed payment exception. The instruction still asks for the wrong thing, so new kinds of nitpick keep arriving.
d.tempting: It is quick and needs no change to the prompt.

concept: Explicit criteria beat vague instructions. State exactly which categories to report and which to skip, rather than leaving the model to infer what "robust" or "accurate" means. A high false-positive rate in one category also undermines trust in the accurate ones.
Claude follows explicit instructions, so say what to do and, where it helps, what to skip. Explaining why a rule exists helps Claude generalise it.

lessons.explanation: The written rule does not tell the reviewer where acceptable `float` use ends and a genuine money bug begins. A few varied examples with their reasoning show that line: a display-only chart is skipped, settlement arithmetic is reported, and a test fixture is skipped. The reviewer then applies the distinction to code it has not seen, inside the one prompt the team must keep.

a.reasoning: Several examples that mix cases to skip and a case to report show where the line falls, and the reasoning lets the reviewer carry it to new code. This covers the ambiguity the written rule could not express.

b.reasoning: A single example is copied closely and shows nothing about what to leave alone, so the reviewer may flag the charts again. Examples that include acceptable cases are what carry the distinction.
b.tempting: The settlement bug is the case that matters, so one clear example looks enough.

d.tempting: Specialised prompts per kind of file sound more precise.

lessons.explanation: Two noisy categories are damaging trust in two accurate ones, and the team needs both quick relief and a lasting fix. Pausing the performance and comment-accuracy categories removes most of the noise now while security and bug findings keep their value. Rewriting their criteria to say what to report and what to skip fixes the cause, and each category comes back once its false positives drop.

a.reasoning: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated unless it is checked against labelled data, so a threshold would not separate wrong findings from right ones. It could also hide real security findings, and no criteria would change.
a.tempting: A confidence cut-off is a cheap way to trade volume for accuracy.

b.reasoning: A category with a high false-positive rate undermines trust in the accurate ones. Switching the two noisy categories off for now restores trust this sprint and leaves security and bug findings running.

c.reasoning: Rewriting the criteria is the right fix, but leaving the categories live keeps a 55% to 62% false-positive rate in front of developers this sprint. Trust returns when they are paused first and re-enabled once they are accurate.
c.tempting: Developers would see the improved wording working in live reviews.

d.reasoning: The noise comes from vague criteria, so the lasting fix is explicit report-and-skip rules. Re-enabling each category only after it proves accurate keeps developers from losing trust again.

e.reasoning: The reviewer rereading its own comments keeps the reasoning that produced them and rarely questions it. It adds a stage without addressing the unclear criteria.
e.tempting: A self-check step looks like a cheap way to remove doubtful comments.

concept: When one category has a high false-positive rate, temporarily disable it so the accurate categories keep developers' trust, and rewrite its criteria to state what to report and what to skip. Turn it back on once it proves accurate.

lessons.explanation: The audit has a 36-hour deadline, and a batch can take up to 24 hours with no promised completion time. The worst case is the wait for the next submission plus the full 24-hour window, and both must fit inside the deadline. Submitting every 6 hours gives 6 + 24 = 30 hours, which fits, and the job keeps the batch discount because nothing waits on it interactively.

a.reasoning: A change merged just after 02:00 waits almost 24 hours and then up to 24 more, about 48 hours in the worst case. That breaks the 36-hour rule, however non-interactive the audit is.
a.tempting: The audit is not interactive, so the cheapest option should do.

b.reasoning: Batching more often is the right idea, but 18 hours of waiting plus up to 24 hours of batch time is 42 hours, over the limit. The submission interval must be short enough for wait plus processing to fit.
b.tempting: It still batches more often and keeps the discount.

c.reasoning: The Message Batches API has no priority setting and no latency guarantee. It trades a discount for a window of up to 24 hours, so the submission frequency must be planned around that.
c.tempting: A priority setting would make the nightly plan meet the deadline.

concept: The Message Batches API charges 50% of standard prices in exchange for a processing window of up to 24 hours and no guaranteed latency. Most batches finish within an hour, but a batch not done in 24 hours expires.

lessons.explanation: The session that wrote a fix is not the best judge of it, because it keeps the reasoning that produced the code and is less likely to question it. A separate `claude -p` instance that receives the diff and the review criteria but none of that reasoning reads the change critically and catches subtler issues. It still runs before the merge and adds no human step.

a.reasoning: Extra thinking in the same session still starts from the reasoning that wrote the fix, so the model tends to confirm its own choices. A longer chain of thought does not replace a fresh perspective.
a.tempting: More reasoning time should make the self-review more thorough.

b.reasoning: A separate instance without the author's reasoning is not anchored to the choices that produced the code. The diff and criteria give it enough context for a pre-merge review.

c.reasoning: A separate instance is the right shape, but handing it the transcript passes on the author's reasoning and anchors the reviewer to the same choices. Independence comes from not seeing that reasoning.
c.tempting: The transcript explains why each change was made, which looks useful context.

d.reasoning: A generic instruction to write correct code and test it is a nudge, not a review, and the generator would still judge its own work. It adds no independent check.
d.tempting: Better code from the generator means fewer flawed fixes.

concept: A model reviewing its own output keeps the reasoning from generation and is less likely to question its decisions. Review from a clean context, with none of the session's history, using an independent instance.
Independent review instances without the generator's reasoning catch subtler issues than self-review. Give the reviewer the diff and the criteria, not the author's reasoning.

lessons.explanation: The Batches API fits work nothing waits on and that is a single request each. A weekly audit and a nightly test-generation job both tolerate a window of up to 24 hours and save up to 50%. A blocking merge check and an interactive assistant need quick replies, and a job that needs a tool result partway through a request cannot run inside one batch request.

a.reasoning: Nobody waits on a weekly audit, so a processing window of up to 24 hours costs nothing and the discount is pure saving. It is the kind of latency-tolerant work the Batches API is for.

b.reasoning: A blocking check cannot wait up to 24 hours for a result with no latency guarantee. A pre-merge check needs synchronous calls even though they cost more.

c.reasoning: The timing suits a batch, but each batch request is an independent call and cannot make a mid-request tool round trip. The ticket text would need to be fetched and included beforehand.
c.tempting: The nightly timing is ideal for a batch.

d.reasoning: An interactive assistant needs a reply in seconds and a batch may take hours. The saving does not justify breaking a live conversation.
d.tempting: Interactive traffic is the largest volume, so it saves the most.

e.reasoning: Overnight generation has a built-in gap before anyone needs the output, so batch latency is acceptable. Each request is a single prompt, and `custom_id` can carry the file path to match results.

concept: Batch the requests no one waits on, such as overnight reports, weekly audits and nightly test generation. Keep a check that a merge waits on on standard, synchronous calls.

lessons.explanation: An exclusion list is always one step behind, because nitpicks come in unlimited kinds, which is why the dismissed share fell only from 41% to 34%. Defining the review by what to report gives a closed scope: security flaws and bugs that fail on a stated input, each with an example, and everything else is out of scope. c.reasoning: Naming narrow categories to report gives a closed scope, so new nitpicks are excluded without a new rule. Concrete examples for each category show what meets the bar.

d.tempting: A second pass can classify and delete the nitpicks automatically.

lessons.explanation: The reviewer does not know that `SafeLogger` and `Money` are the team's intended wrappers, so it calls them non-standard. lessons.explanation: The four document types share almost no fields and each has its own extraction rules, so one wide schema and prompt invites values to leak between them. A short classification call that routes each document to a prompt and schema written for its type removes the cross-type fields by construction. The extra call is small next to a long combined prompt, so it also suits 30,000 documents a night.

a.reasoning: Separating the types gives each its own schema and rules, so a repair invoice can no longer receive a `billing_code` from a part number. Each type-specific prompt stays small and testable.

b.reasoning: Examples help with ambiguous formats, but this prompt already holds 12 and the wide schema still offers every field on every document. The types need separate schemas and rules, not another layer in one prompt.
b.tempting: More examples with null fields would show the model the right pattern for each type.

c.reasoning: `any` guarantees that some tool is called, not that the right fields are filled. The leakage comes from one schema covering four document types, so forcing a call changes nothing.
c.tempting: Making the tool call certain should make the extraction tidy.

d.reasoning: Both runs share the same prompt and schema, so they leak the same fields and agree with each other. It doubles the cost on 30,000 documents without separating the types.
d.tempting: Agreement between two runs looks like a reliability check.

concept: When document types need different schemas and extraction rules, classify first and route to a type-specific prompt and schema. A schema that offers every field on every document invites values in the wrong place.

A tool definition has a name, a description and an input schema. `tool_choice` set to `auto` is the default, `any` must use one of the tools and `tool` forces a named tool; none of these separates document types. Model caveat: on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and the Fable/Mythos 5.x models, `any` and forced `tool` return a 400 error, so there `tool_choice` stays on `auto`. The exam guide still teaches `any` and forced selection, so this lesson keeps the exam's answer.

lessons.explanation: "Flag claims that look suspicious" leaves the model to judge by impression, so it flags ordinary claims with a late filing or a high repair bill. lessons.explanation: A strict schema removes syntax errors, not semantic ones, so a total that differs from the sum of the line items still gets through. Extracting the printed figure as `stated_total`, adding a model-summed `calculated_total` and a `conflict_detected` boolean makes the disagreement visible and attributable. The pipeline can then route each conflict to review with both figures.

a.reasoning: Schema validity covers structure and types, not arithmetic between fields, and a schema cannot compare two values. A rule that rejected mismatches would also hide printed-total errors instead of exposing them.
a.tempting: A schema rule would enforce the arithmetic automatically.

b.reasoning: A calculated total is part of the fix, but dropping the printed figure hides the conflict. If a line item was misread the wrong sum becomes the total, and an error on the invoice goes unnoticed.
b.tempting: One field cannot disagree with itself.

c.reasoning: Capturing both figures makes the disagreement visible, so a reviewer starts with the numbers instead of the scan. The boolean lets the pipeline route conflicts automatically.

d.reasoning: Retrying until two numbers agree rewards agreement, not accuracy, and if the printed total is wrong no retry will change it. It adds calls for a problem that needs surfacing.
d.tempting: Retrying should eventually give an extraction where the totals agree.

concept: Strict schemas remove syntax errors but not semantic errors such as line items that do not sum or values in the wrong field. A validator checks what the schema cannot, such as arithmetic across fields.
Self-correction fields, such as `calculated_total` beside `stated_total` and a `conflict_detected` boolean, expose semantic conflicts so the pipeline can act on them.

lessons.explanation: Required fields push the model to invent a value when the document has none, which is where `"UNKNOWN"` and `1970-01-01` come from. Making the fields nullable gives it an honest way to report absence, and routing documents with no service data to reviewers handles the gap without a retry. A validator rule that rejects placeholders catches slips.

a.reasoning: Required fields push the model to invent a value when the document has none. A nullable field gives it a truthful way to report absence, which is the root of the placeholders.

b.reasoning: A retry with feedback helps with format errors but cannot recover information that is not in the document. The model would only invent a plausible code to satisfy the retry.
b.tempting: Appending the error should push the model to look harder.

c.reasoning: Forcing a tool makes the model call it, but it does not create information, so the required fields would still be filled with something. Model caveat: on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and the Fable/Mythos 5.x models, `any` and forced `tool` return a 400 error, so there `tool_choice` stays on `auto`. The exam guide still teaches `any` and forced selection, so this lesson keeps the exam's answer.
c.tempting: Making the tool call certain should force a real value.

d.reasoning: The information is not in these documents, so a retry would only pressure the model to guess again. Routing them to reviewers deals with the gap, and a rule against placeholders catches slips.

e.tempting: Blank and zero values look less suspicious than the placeholders.

concept: Nullable fields prevent fabrication: when a required field has no value in the document, the model invents one. A nullable field, or an `"unclear"` or `"other"` value with a detail string, lets it say so honestly.

Retries help with format errors and do not help when the information is absent from the source. Documents that lack the information belong with reviewers. With a nullable field, requests that lack the fact came back null.

lessons.explanation: The Batches API trades a discount for a processing window of up to 24 hours and no latency guarantee. lessons.explanation: On retry the model got the failed JSON and the validator message but not the bill, so it can only make the numbers agree, not check them against the source. lessons.explanation: A `stop_reason` of `max_tokens` means the output was cut at the cap, and the 150-line-item array does not fit in 4096 tokens, so the JSON stops mid-array and will not parse. `max_tokens` caps the length of the response, not the context window. The fix is a higher cap for these requests, and treating any response that stops at `max_tokens` as a failure so a truncated one is never parsed.

a.reasoning: `max_tokens` caps the length of the response, and a stop reason of `max_tokens` means the output was cut at that cap. The long array needs more output room, and the pipeline should reject a truncated response.

b.reasoning: A shorter answer would fit, but adjudication needs every line item, so required data would be lost. The documents genuinely need a long output, so the limit has to change.
b.tempting: Returning only the total and top items keeps the JSON small and valid.

c.reasoning: The invoice fits in the context window with room to spare, so the window is not what stopped the response. It stopped because of `max_tokens`, which caps the length of the output.
c.tempting: A bigger window looks like more room for long documents.

d.reasoning: Retrying with feedback helps with format errors, but the same 4096-token cap cuts the same output on every attempt. The retries add cost and still produce unparseable JSON.
d.tempting: A parse error is a validation failure that a retry can fix.

concept: `max_tokens` caps the length of the response. A `stop_reason` of `max_tokens` means the output was cut at that cap, so it may not match the schema even when a strict schema is used.

Extracting both values into separate fields and adding a `conflict_detected` boolean turns the hidden disagreement into something the pipeline can act on. Flagged forms go to the review queue, so the claim is not bounced to the customer.

a.reasoning: Rejecting the whole claim over a recoverable inconsistency delays a customer for a problem a reviewer can resolve. The other extracted fields are still good.

b.reasoning: Capturing both values is right, but choosing the earlier date in code resolves the conflict silently. The earlier date is not always the correct one, and nobody learns the form disagreed with itself.
b.tempting: Keeping the earlier date is a simple, predictable rule.

c.reasoning: Capturing both values with an explicit conflict flag turns a hidden disagreement into a field the pipeline can act on. Reviewers receive the forms that need a decision.

d.reasoning: Three runs triple the cost and still resolve the conflict silently. The disagreement is in the document, so every run sees both dates.
d.tempting: A majority vote among runs picks the most likely date.

concept: Contradictions in a source should surface, not be picked silently. Capture both conflicting values and add a `conflict_detected` boolean so the pipeline can route the form to review.
Semantic conflicts are different from schema syntax errors: a strict schema removes syntax errors but cannot tell that two fields disagree, so the schema needs fields that expose the conflict.

lessons.explanation: The checker receives the first instance's JSON and is asked to confirm it, so it is anchored to that answer and confirms 99% of fields. An independent instance that extracts the fields on its own, without seeing the first result, has no stake in it. Comparing the two outputs sends only the disagreements to the reviewers, so their workload does not grow.

a.reasoning: Passing the generator's reasoning makes the checker adopt the same assumptions, which weakens its independence further. An independent view needs less of the author's context.
a.tempting: Knowing why each value was chosen should help the checker judge it.

b.reasoning: A clean instance removes history, but it still reads the first instance's JSON and is asked to confirm it. The anchoring comes from seeing the first answer, so the checker stays biased toward approving it.
b.tempting: A fresh instance per claim avoids carrying over any bias.

c.reasoning: An anchored checker's confidence is poorly calibrated, since it already agreed with 99% of fields. It would approve the same errors with less visibility than now.
c.tempting: A high threshold should pass only the surest fields.

d.reasoning: Seeing the first answer anchors the checker toward confirming it. An independent extraction has no stake in the first result, and the disagreements are the only items the reviewers need to see.

concept: An independent second instance catches subtler issues than a reviewer that sees the first result. A model that sees the first answer is less likely to question it, so have the second instance work without it and compare the outputs.
Self-reported confidence alongside a finding is a verification aid, not a threshold to filter by. Raw confidence is unreliable unless calibrated.

A reviewer works best from a clean context, with none of the author's history. A checker shown the first instance's answer is anchored to that answer in the same way a session reviewing its own change is.
